Turning Edge AI Data Into Real-Time Action

3

Shares

3

On-device AI can deliver faster insights, greater autonomy, and less cloud traffic — but only with the right infrastructure.

October 1st, 2026 -

By: Liz Allan

Key Takeaways:

Edge AI is expanding across consumer, industrial, automotive, and medical devices by moving real-time intelligence closer to where data is generated.
Edge analytics systems deliver value only when edge devices have the right deployment, monitoring, lifecycle management, and software infrastructure.
Security, power efficiency, connectivity, and memory choices must be designed in from the start as edge AI systems take on more autonomous decision-making roles.

More AI is moving out of centralized data centers and into devices that can interpret data and act on it in real time.
By handling more processing locally, these edge systems can sharply reduce latency, improve security and privacy, and address growing concerns about data center energy and water consumption. Some data is already processed locally in consumer, industrial, automotive, and medical applications, but that percentage is expected to grow significantly in the next few years as edge devices become more capable and smaller language models are introduced.
“Number one are your personal devices,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA. “Those are small. For example, a watch that can track your ECG and so forth. If your heartbeat rhythm is off, you can set it up so that it calls your hospital directly. On the industrial side, for example, a control unit monitors pressure in a boiler, or a control unit monitors a particular assembly line in a given section of an automotive factory. At the very extreme edges, every time a robot is picking up something and doing something, the finger is an edge device.”
Vehicles contain multiple sensors and processors that process data locally. “I would say cars in general are not edge devices,” said Balasubramanian. “Edge devices are more like the lidar in the car. Lidar finds out all your obstacles and everything, then it needs to be processed on board the car. Every section of the car is an edge device, whether it’s radar, lidar, the camera, or what is sensing in the camera, which needs to make sense of what the camera is seeing. That whole system is an edge device.”
The medical space is also filled with intelligent edge devices. “For example, a robotic surgeon has arms and knows the position to make the cut, with the right pressure,” said Balasubramanian. “Then all the systems need to be monitored and connected so that if the patient’s heart rate goes up, or they are trying to wake up, the human needs to figure out what to do.”
Whatever the application, edge AI analytics focus on real-time performance and metrics that address how data is gathered, stored, and used, as well as what actions are taken based on that data. That information is then looped back to improve the process. In effect, edge AI analytics systems act as a bridge between different systems, and between people and hardware.
“By placing compute near data sources, edge AI infrastructure enables local inference across telecom nodes, industrial gateways, enterprise servers, and smart building controllers,” said William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence. “These systems operate at the point of physical interaction, powering applications from automotive and industrial SoCs to wearables, smart cameras, and consumer endpoints.”
That connection between local intelligence and physical systems depends on a steady flow of usable data, collected close to the source, and filtered before it moves farther upstream.
Data comes from numerous devices and sensors. “From a data‑gathering perspective, edge systems primarily ingest information from two sources — sensors and human or agent interactions,” Chen explained. “Sensors span a wide range of modalities, including vision via cameras, light, environmental, industrial, and more. They generate data at very high volumes and speeds. Examples include multi‑camera video streams captured over millisecond‑scale intervals — or faster. To make this data tractable, raw sensor outputs must be processed locally to reduce bandwidth and latency requirements before being forwarded upstream, either to a local compute cluster or directly to a cloud‑based AI factory for higher‑level processing and reasoning.”
Setting up an edge AI analytics system
Several key considerations come into play when deploying an integrated edge AI analytics system.
“Organizations building edge AI systems will gain a durable advantage by tightly integrating compute, data movement, interfaces, and security models early,” Chen noted. “Once collected, all data must be transported efficiently for downstream or upstream processing steps such as reasoning, inference, and storage. These data paths span multiple hops and domains — from sensors to edge processors, between edge processors and adjunct accelerators or local memory, from edge devices to gateways, and ultimately from gateways to cloud infrastructure.”
Layers of software oversee all these elements, from digital twins to product lifecycle management.
“The key challenge is, how do you build a model for what the edge AI needs to do?” said Balasubramanian. “The second thing is, how do you connect the entire digital thread with what we see in the digital twin of the product to the digital twin in the factory? Then, how do you monitor everything, and how do you do the analytics? Finally, how do you act on it?”
Balasubramanian described three components to this flow:

An open digital business platform that lets companies of any size work together to solve industrial challenges;
A product lifecycle management (PLM) software platform that helps organizations manage all data, processes, and documentation for a product from its initial design through manufacturing, service, and disposal; and
Edge devices deployed throughout the facility gathering data. These can include fixed sensor devices, robots, cobots, autonomous mobile robots, or an industrial arm in a production line.

Silicon lifecycle management (SLM) can provide additional device-level monitoring, while PLM serves as the data backbone of an edge analytics system.
“You can essentially trace back everything,” said Balasubramanian. “When I ordered this part, what maintenance was done on the part on this robot? When was the last firmware update done? Who came and accessed the data? Was anything different in this particular robot compared to everything else in the factory flow?”
Edge AI devices can use local processing to make decisions, or some combination of local, near-local, and cloud. But the ability to act locally is only useful if the surrounding infrastructure is configured to control where data moves, how models are deployed, and when humans remain part of the decision loop.
Systems administrators need to deploy edge devices effectively to benefit from analytics. “Companies want to have more edge-based analytics for the purpose of keeping their data on their own localized systems, so they would set up the infrastructure to enable that to happen,” said Matthew Bubis, director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “There would be a human in the loop to set that up, but once it’s set up, a company or an enterprise might have an automated system of managing that. For example, if you open your company laptop and you’re using an AI-based system, the IT department would have set up a way to manage really sensitive, secure data. They would put a wrapper on that to say, ‘We must process this on the edge and deploy to the edge systems only so that we’re keeping all our data closed.’ The data is automated, but that’s after a human has decided how the edge devices operate.”
The overall goal of edge AI analytics is to improve the organization’s operations. “AI is increasingly moving from the digital world into the physical world, where it can improve how systems operate, make decisions, and use resources more efficiently,” said Stephan Zizala, division president of edge systems at Infineon Technologies. “The next wave of innovation will not be defined by how much data we collect, but by how effectively we can turn that data into action. Across industries, organizations are looking for ways to improve operations through faster insights, greater efficiency, and more autonomous decision-making. Edge AI enables that shift by processing data close to where it is generated, whether from sensors in industrial equipment, smart homes, or robots. This allows systems to react in real time, reduces dependence on constant cloud connectivity, and helps keep sensitive information under local control.”
How those systems are connected depends on the operating environment, the sensitivity of the data, and the balance each organization wants to strike between autonomy, control, and cloud-based scale.
On one end, semiconductor fabs may keep their analytics systems air-gapped, so no data gets in or out. On the other end, a soda bottling facility may run entirely in the cloud for efficiency. Often, it’s a combination of both. “You will have a local model doing more of the regular work, but it is not working constantly all the time,” said Balasubramanian. “This is similar to how humans sleep and think through the day and get the brain to realign all the memories and skills. At some point, you will phone in to the cloud and update the models. Or if they come up with some corner cases, you need to be able to update the learning of the main model. For example, Tesla updates the software of the car.”
Edge analytics security considerations
Protecting proprietary IP is important, along with privacy, because applications such as wearables handle personal data.
“In parallel to sensor data, data generated through human or agent interaction includes inputs from AI assistants, via local inference models, as well as corrections, feedback, or direct inputs from end users,” said Cadence’s Chen. “These workflows drive a strong need for privacy‑controlled edge environments, where sensitive information is retained in secure local storage and only ‘must‑have’ and conditioned data, which has been filtered, encrypted, and policy‑controlled, is transmitted to the cloud.”
Security must be considered at every layer, or organizations risk impacting human worker safety in addition to financial loss through downtime or fraud.
The analytics layer needs specific attention. “For example, with the software that processes data and detects anomalies, triggers, and prioritizes alerts, the risks are related to decision integrity,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Analytics systems risk missing the real problems, failing to detect abnormalities, such as in a medical setting where signs of patient health deterioration are missed. It could also be fraud or equipment failures. In any of these settings, too many alerts can be created, similar to false positives, where there are repeated incorrect patient alerts. Other risks include the corruption of the analytics model itself, including hidden backdoors that allow specific untrusted users to be trusted.”
Edge analytics fleet management platforms and alert systems also face compromise. “For example, by allowing malicious updates, model deployment, or manipulation of a whole fleet of devices,” said Neustadter. “These types of platforms have a large — maybe one of the largest — attack surfaces, and are becoming high-value targets because edge AI deployments rely on them for device onboarding, AI model deployments and management, alerts, analytics, and policy management. There are also software supply-chain attacks, such as compromising models or updates of infrastructure even before deployment.”
Edge AI devices also bring specific security risks. “The biggest shift in edge AI security is that cyber attackers are moving from trying to steal information to trying to manipulate decisions,” Neustadter observed. “Edge devices are evolving to autonomous decision-makers, where a successful attack can influence not just the data collection, but real-world actions.”
Verifiable trust is needed across the entire lifecycle, from device authenticity and software integrity to data provenance, model integrity, and secure management, Neustadter explained. “AI model compromise includes adversarial attacks, poisoning, extraction, and unauthorized modifications.”
A recent NIST publication identified adversarial machine learning as a major emerging security concern. “For example, attackers intentionally manipulate inputs to cause AI systems to make incorrect decisions while appearing normal to humans,” said Neustadter. [1] “Model theft is another example because AI models themselves are valuable assets as companies invest significantly to differentiate in the market and secure business.
AI reliability/safety must also be considered, especially for medical devices, industrial automation, robotics, and autonomous devices. “An incorrect AI recommendation can create safety or operational consequences even if there is no malicious intent,” she noted. “Unlike traditional software, AI systems can make incorrect decisions even if no attacks have occurred.”
Those security and reliability requirements ultimately flow back into silicon choices, because edge processors must support local intelligence while meeting tight constraints on power, latency, connectivity, and trust.
Edge AI processing chips
A programmable logic controller (PLC), which generally consists of a microprocessor (MPU) with a CPU, memory, and interface ICs, acts as a bridge between the sensors and AI. The AI could be processed by a low-power MCU, NPU (neural), or VPU (vision).
“There will be an MCU, but also the PLC running industrial edge,” said Balasubramanian. “A virtual PLC is already security-proven, so you could have that in the edge as part of your system to run and monitor everything based on what you’re getting from the PLM (product lifecycle management) thread and what you’re getting from real-time data.”
GPUs also have a role to play. “Traditionally, AI was always these huge, giant, data center-level cards going everywhere,” said Imagination’s Bubis. “But now we are implementing AI processing technology within our very smallest chips, because we see small chip edge AI customers who might have a tiny device in a television or a refrigerator for the home.”
While matrix multiplication tasks are important, edge AI GPUs are also needed for traditional graphics processing tasks. For example, a robot may have a display screen so a maintenance worker can see what’s going on. “We see the dual use case in edge AI,” said Bubis. “In automotive, that’s 100% the case, because you’ve got these ever-larger screens and displays demanding very complex graphics outputs whilst also demanding some AI workloads, either for ADAS or for the local LLMs that might be happening in the vehicle.”
In enterprise and client applications, various devices and widgets process data locally, with small language models and AI bots saving IT personnel time by fielding basic questions. “Extendable platforms can be connected to single-board computers to provide the ability to run heavy compute,” said Bubis.
Those processing choices also shape the surrounding data fabric, because edge AI systems must move information among sensors, accelerators, memory, and networks quickly enough to support real-time analytics.
Networking and memory for edge analytics
Compute, interfaces, and memory all play a key role in edge analytics.
“How to move data reliably and efficiently has become just as important as increasing compute capability in edge AI system design,” said Cadence’s Chen. “Long adopted in the mobile system, MIPI CSI-2 serves as a preferred vision ingress interface in embedded systems, along with other USB-based and proprietary links, efficiently feeding image data into the ISP pipeline and aligning well with edge device requirements. Beyond vision, many interface protocols foundational to modern cloud AI factory architectures, such as PCIe, Ethernet, LPDDR/DDR/GDDR, and UCIe, are increasingly deployed at the edge because of their proven topologies and mature ecosystems. Given the constraints typical of edge platforms, however, designs are strongly biased toward cost‑ and power‑efficient implementations.”
UCIe and PCIe are both utilized. “Although UCIe is commonly viewed as a premium interconnect for high‑end AI and chiplet-centric designs, heterogeneous execution at the edge is emerging and potentially relevant for future edge designs,” said Chen. “The modularity, flexibility, and reuse enabled by chiplet architectures are increasingly compelling for edge applications that demand tailored and heterogeneous I/O mixes. PCIe 3/4/5 plays a central role in attaching high‑throughput peripherals such as accelerators, NVMe storage, and NICs, while the long‑established Ethernet standards remain widely deployed and form the backbone of most edge networking environments, ranging from 1G to 10G for devices to 25G–100G for infrastructure.”
Memory can also be heterogeneous. “In memory subsystems, a practical mix of DDR5, GDDR6/7, and LPDDR5X/6 has been increasingly adopted in higher-performance edge systems, optimizing capacity, bandwidth, and energy efficiency across diverse edge use cases,” said Chen.
While HBM and DDR may be the right choice for high-performance systems, LPDDR is a common choice for edge and embedded AI, where energy efficiency and cost are important, according to Rambus. Applications include computer vision, robotics, industrial automation, medical devices, and battery-powered or thermally constrained systems. The memory controller must be optimized for low-power operation, work across challenging conditions, and integrate flexibly into diverse SoC architectures.
Also, an edge-optimized network architecture should deliver packet-level visibility, active monitoring, and application intelligence to ensure tools never miss a thing, according to Keysight.
 
Fig. 1: An edge-optimized network. Source: Keysight
Conclusion
Edge AI is a fast-growing space, particularly in the industrial sector, with new devices and use cases emerging all the time.
“The excitement I have is coming up with different designs and edge devices,” said Balasubramanian. “We are seeing a lot of momentum in putting intelligent devices at the edge — not just sensors, but real devices. That’s an entire system that can operate on its own, either air-gapped or connected to the internet, Wi-Fi, or the cloud. That’s the beauty of it. Essentially, you have everything connected to something, and it already has its own brain to operate.”
Edge AI systems need to take corrective action very quickly. “If it takes a lot of time to process and correct the mistake, then you might have a lot of defective parts already done in a car manufacturing factory, or in a GPU manufacturing fab, and everywhere else,” said Balasubramanian. “The goal is to have fewer humans involved in the factory, but to have more domain specialists monitoring it much more smartly, so that there is no downtime and the quality is always 100%. That’s the kind of metric that industrial teams look at.”
An end-to-end deployment flow is key. “As AI continues its journey into the physical world, sensors, intelligence, connectivity, and security must work together seamlessly,” said Infineon’s Zizala. “The real opportunity lies in creating systems that not only collect data but can understand their environment and act on it intelligently, reliably, and securely.”
